content: Children aged 12 months or older who are living with HIV and are unlikely to have active tuberculosis (TB) based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines should be offered TB preventive treatment (TPT) as part of a comprehensive HIV prevention and care package. This is particularly important in settings with high TB transmission, regardless of whether they have been in contact with a person with TB. Children living with HIV who have successfully completed treatment for TB disease may also receive TPT. Additionally, children under 5 years old who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have active TB after clinical evaluation should be given TPT, even if latent TB infection (LTBI) testing is unavailable. For children aged 5 years or older, adolescents, and adults who are household contacts of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB and are found not to have active TB, TPT may also be provided. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, or a persistent cough, or who have a history of contact with a person with TB, should be evaluated for TB and other diseases causing these symptoms. If active TB is excluded after appropriate evaluation, these children should be offered TPT regardless of their age. The absence of TB symptoms and normal chest radiographic findings can be used to rule out active TB disease in HIV-negative household contacts aged 5 years or older and other at-risk groups before initiating preventive treatment. Testing for LTBI can be done using either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA). For the treatment of LTBI, the following regimens are recommended regardless of HIV status: 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, a 3-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a 3-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Alternative options include a 1-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or 4 months of daily rifampicin alone. In high TB transmission settings, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have an unknown or positive LTBI test and are unlikely to have active TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). This should be provided regardless of whether the individual is on antiretroviral therapy (ART), their degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy status. TB among pregnant women is associated with a six-fold increase in perinatal deaths and a two-fold risk of premature birth and low birth weight. HIV co-infection further increases the risk of maternal and infant mortality by nearly 300%. Therefore, TB treatment should be initiated promptly in pregnant women when the probability of TB is moderate to high. Systematic screening for active TB should be part of antenatal care, and diagnosis and treatment should be provided promptly when indicated. TB diagnosis in pregnant women follows the same protocols as for other adults, with TST and chest radiography (with appropriate shielding) being safe options. Most TB medications are not harmful to the fetus, although some, such as amikacin, streptomycin, ethionamide, and prothionamide, are contraindicated during pregnancy. Treatment for drug-resistant TB in pregnant women should be individualized and carefully managed by specialized services, with counseling on potential risks to the fetus. After delivery, breastfeeding should not be discouraged, as the concentration of TB drugs in breast milk is too low to harm the newborn. People living with HIV are at a significantly higher risk of developing TB disease, dying from it, and experiencing recurrent TB after being cured. TB is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among people living with HIV. Pulmonary sputum smear-negative and extrapulmonary forms of TB are common in this population, making diagnosis challenging. Advanced diagnostic tools, such as molecular WHO-approved rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) and lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan assay (LF-LAM), should be made available. TB treatment in people living with HIV requires careful management to address potential interactions between TB and antiretroviral drugs. When TB and HIV are diagnosed simultaneously, TB treatment should be initiated first, followed by ART within the first two weeks of TB treatment, regardless of CD4 count. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) may occur during this period and requires experienced clinical management. Drug-resistant TB in people living with HIV is associated with higher mortality, emphasizing the need for early diagnosis, prompt treatment initiation, and close monitoring. Adverse effects from TB and antiretroviral drugs should be closely monitored, and management should be overseen by specialists. Adjustments to ART may be necessary to address drug interactions, with priority given to treating the life-threatening condition. Nutritional status plays a critical role in TB outcomes. Undernutrition weakens the immune system, increasing the risk of developing TB and worsening treatment outcomes. TB itself can cause severe weight loss due to reduced appetite, nausea, and metabolic changes. Nutritional assessment and support should be integral to TB care, with interventions tailored to individual needs. Weight gain during TB treatment is a positive sign of response and may require dosage adjustments for TB medications. Nutritional counseling and support are cost-effective investments that improve treatment adherence and outcomes.
